paras: The threatened lynching at Harriman, Tennessee, was an August 1895 manhunt in which armed searching parties and police bloodhounds pursued a Black man accused of assaulting a young white girl, while newspapers reported he would be lynched if caught. A man arrested in Atlanta, named in most reports as George Gaither, was returned amid rumors of a posse and released when the girl failed to identify him. Nearly fifty Black men were arrested on suspicion; no lynching was reported.

According to a Chattanooga wire dated August 4, the girl was the 12-year-old daughter of a farmer living near Harriman and was attacked on her way home from Sunday school that day. A Steubenville, Ohio, correspondent wrote that the family had come from Ohio several years earlier and named the father Darwin Rex. The first wire called the father James Redwhite, while later dispatches named the girl Myrtle Rex and her father H. M. Rex, "a leading citizen of Harriman."

The wire reports said a Black man met the girl in the road, threatened her with death if she cried out, dragged her into the bushes and escaped before she could alert anyone. The same dispatch said "the neighborhood is alive with searching parties, and if captured he will be lynched at once," and that an officer with bloodhounds had left Chattanooga for Harriman that night. Late that night two Black men were arrested, one of them believed to be the man sought, and the wire said that if the child identified him "it will be all over with him shortly."

A Washington Evening Star special of August 6 said Harriman had telegraphed Chattanooga's police chief for three bloodhounds, that its citizens were "threatening a lynching should he be captured," and that Officer Smith had left with the hounds. The Ohio account said the girl's father and neighbors "quickly armed themselves and started in pursuit." A wire of the same date put the hounds on a trail toward Lenoir and said "the talk of lynching has ceased." An August 9 Chattanooga item said officers had "just caught the negro" accused and that a lynching was possible, without naming him.

On August 12 a Marshal Long and a deputy who had followed a Black man from Harriman had him arrested on the Atlanta exposition grounds, according to a dispatch naming him Milton Dother. Long feared "an attempt will be made to lynch the negro." A Chattanooga special printed August 14 named him George Gather, said a sheriff had taken charge of him near Harriman, and declared that "lynching is sure today," with a posse rumored on its way to take him out.

A Knoxville dispatch of August 14 reported that Gaither had been released that morning because the girl failed to identify him, and that nearly fifty Black men had been arrested on suspicion. No report of a later arrest, a trial or a lynching appears in the coverage.

Only white newspapers carried the case, through wires from Chattanooga, Atlanta and Knoxville. The first reports called the accused a "fiend" and "ravisher" and treated lynching as the likely end, under headlines such as "IT WILL BE ALL OVER" (Birmingham Age-Herald) and "BLOODHOUNDS AFTER A RAVISHER" (Savannah Morning News). When the Atlanta suspect was brought back, the Age-Herald ran "ALMOST SURE TO SWING" and the Morning News "RAPIST SURE TO BE LYNCHED," both calling him "the negro rapist" before the girl had seen him. That story added that the girl "had been raised in the north to believe in negro virtue."

His release a day later ran as a short item without comment, under "Girl Fails to Identify Him" in Savannah and "GAITHER RELEASED" in Birmingham. Shortened versions ran in the Scranton Tribune, the Richmond Times and the Maysville Daily Public Ledger, with names garbled as "James Red," "Myrtle Reed" and "Myrtle Hex."

Most reports gave the girl's age as 12, but the Atlanta dispatch said 14 and the Chattanooga special of August 13 said 9. The Atlanta prisoner was called Milton Dother in one dispatch and George Gather or Gaither in others, and his arrest was credited to Marshal Long in one and to an Atlanta detective in another.

bases: Armed searching parties and residents hunted an accused Black man and were reported ready to lynch him if caught, and a posse was rumored to be going to take a later suspect from jail, but no killing was reported (A1, A5, A10, A13).

Searching parties and townspeople threatened to lynch the accused man for an alleged assault on a white girl (A1, A5, A10), but no one was reported killed; the suspect brought back from Atlanta was released when the girl failed to identify him (A16).

Separate Chattanooga wire, Washington Evening Star special and Steubenville special agree on the alleged assault near Harriman, the armed search and the lynching threats (A1, A5, A10), and later Atlanta, Chattanooga and Knoxville dispatches follow the arrest and release of a suspect (A12, A13, A16).

framing.detail: Headlines 'IT WILL BE ALL OVER' and 'BLOODHOUNDS AFTER A RAVISHER ... His Doom Is Sealed' treated lynching as the expected end and called the accused a 'fiend' and 'villain'.
'ALMOST SURE TO SWING' and 'RAPIST SURE TO BE LYNCHED' named Gather 'the negro rapist' before any identification and said lynching was 'sure today'.
The release ran as short wire items ('Girl Fails to Identify Him', 'GAITHER RELEASED') without comment.

Later reports and the Ohio account use the surname Rex; reprints also give 'James Red'.
